title: Marcos, Australia's Albanese commit to consult on threats to sovereignty
summary: The two countries agreed to consult on contingencies affecting sovereignty and shared security.

blocks.text: Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese (L) walks out with Philippines' President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. after his address to the House of Representatives at the Parliament House in Canberra on February 29, 2024. Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos told Australia's parliament on February 29 that his country was on the "frontline" of a battle against powers undermining regional peace, but would not capitulate in maritime disputes with the likes of China.

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines and Australia agreed on Monday, November 16, to consult each other on contingencies that may affect their sovereignty or shared security interests, a day after the two countries signed a new defense cooperation arrangement in Manila.

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said in a joint statement the two governments would also “consider appropriate measures in response, consistent with our respective processes.”
The joint statement was issued following their bilateral engagement on the sidelines of the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits in Manila.

The two leaders also committed to counter foreign information manipulation and interference, or FIMI, saying they would learn from each other’s experience in promoting “resilient, healthy, and fact-based information environments.” They tied the effort to public awareness of “rights and entitlements under international law.”

South China Sea. On the South China Sea, the leaders said they “remain seriously concerned” about the situation, “particularly the coercive, aggressive, and dangerous actions against Filipino nationals and vessels.” The statement of the two leaders did not name China though Canberra and Manila have both repeatedly accused Beijing of carrying out dangerous actions in the tense waterways.

Marcos and Albanese both reaffirmed that the 2016 arbitral award is “final and binding." The ruling, issued by a tribunal in The Hague in a case brought by Manila, invalidated Beijing’s sweeping claims in the South China Sea. China has refused to recognize it.

The statement follows Sunday’s signing of the Philippines-Australia Defense Cooperation Arrangement. Defense Secretary Gibo Teodoro Jr. and Australian Ambassador Marc Innes-Brown signed the pact at the Manila South Harbor.

According to the joint statement, the arrangement covers maritime domain awareness, littoral operations, logistics and sustainment, cyber defense and secure communications, joint operations planning, force protection and defense infrastructure development.

It replaces a framework that dates back to 1995, and a separate visiting forces agreement in force since 2012 already lets each country’s troops train on the other’s soil. Teodoro has described the new arrangement as a way to cut red tape, saying: "Rather than 100 steps to do a single thing, it will just now take 10."
Albanese on Sunday rejected suggestions that the pact was meant to deter Beijing from further aggression at sea. He said: “This isn’t aimed at any one country."

Manila has been widening its network of security partners, among them Japan and the United States, as confrontations with Chinese vessels in the South China Sea continue. Australia became a strategic partner of the Philippines in 2023, during Albanese’s first visit to Manila.

In Monday’s statement, the two leaders said they would continue maritime cooperative activities in the South China Sea, “bilaterally and with partners,” and share technologies that support maritime domain awareness.

Cybersecurity, cross-border crime. The statement also commits both governments to deepen joint work against terrorism and transnational crime, including drug trafficking, child exploitation, human trafficking and online scam operations. They agreed to strengthen cyber defenses and to keep investigating cybercrime together.
On the economy, Marcos and Albanese said they were committed to open, rules-based trade, “including for essential energy supplies,” and to building more resilient supply chains.
